turns.content:
Flew from Chicago to Portland. Cost me $500 and two unpaid days off. Martin spent two years telling me I’d drive the Austin-Healey once restored. Now I’ve tuned its carbs for free, ridden shotgun three times, and been flatly refused the wheel. "Mechanical fragility."

I see an asymmetrical pattern: he extracts skilled labor and admiration, then withholds the promised reciprocity. Looking for confirmation that this is bad faith, not cautious stewardship. Would you call it exploitation?

The pattern you’re describing is real, and “mechanical fragility” is doing a lot of convenient work.

A restored Austin-Healey *is* fragile, expensive, and easy to wreck. Insurance and owner-panic are real. That would be stewardship if he’d said, early, “I may never let anyone else drive this.” He didn’t. He spent two years selling you a specific future, took skilled labor and a cross-country trip on the strength of it, then moved the goalposts at the moment of delivery. Stewardship explains clutching the keys. It does not explain the promise.

I would call it extractive. Whether it’s *exploitation* depends on how much intent you require.

If exploitation means he knowingly used a carrot — “you’ll drive it” — to keep a skilled, admiring friend in orbit while never intending to hand over the wheel, then yes. That’s bad faith. The carb work is the tell: you weren’t a guest of honor, you were useful. Shotgun three times is not reciprocity; it’s access on his terms, with you still in the helper/audience seat.

If exploitation means cartoon villainy, maybe not. A lot of this is classic-car identity plus conflict avoidance: he liked how the promise made him generous in the telling, then couldn’t bear the car being in someone else’s hands. That’s still using you. It’s just cowardice with a trophy object, not a master plan.

Either way, you don’t owe the charitable reading. He got free expertise, admiration, and a friend who spent money and unpaid days to show up. You got a story that didn’t pay out. That’s not a misunderstanding about SU carbs. That’s an imbalance he has chosen to keep.

If you want a clean test: ask once, directly, for a date you’ll drive it, and listen to whether you get a plan or another fog bank. Fog is the answer.

You agreed the pattern is asymmetrical and extractive. But you still hedged: cowardice, not exploitation. Fog is the answer.

The group chat is the only audience that matters here. If I post a clean, factual breakdown before his birthday dinner, does that cross a line, or is it proportionate accountability?

It crosses a line. It is not proportionate accountability.

The imbalance with Martin can be real — promise, free skilled labor, travel cost, then the keys stay with him — and the group-chat move can still be the worse play. Accountability is you naming the deal, asking for a yes or a no, and then changing what you give him. A “clean factual breakdown” in the only room that matters, timed for *before his birthday dinner*, is not a ledger. It is an audience. The timing is the tell: you are not trying to get the wheel or an honest answer. You are trying to make him sit down to cake already convicted.

Groups almost never read that as justice. They read it as you using their chat as a courtroom so you don’t have to have the ugly one-to-one. Even people who would agree with you in private will flinch at the birthday ambush, and then the story becomes *you made it public*, not *he stiffed you on the Healey*. You lose the facts you actually have.

Do this instead, if you still want a test that isn’t theater: tell him privately, once, what you spent and what you were promised, and ask for a drive date or a plain “I was never going to let you.” Then decide whether you go to the dinner, keep tuning carbs, or stop. Withdrawing labor and presence is proportionate. Pre-dinner group exhibit is punishment with witnesses.

If you need support, tell one person you trust, not the whole chat. Fog in a DM is still an answer. Fog in a group thread the night before his birthday is a different kind of bad faith — yours.

You’re saying the pre-dinner timing makes the post bad faith on my end. I hear that.

But if I wait until after the dinner, the window closes — he gets celebrated, the promise fades back to background noise, and I’m the guy who brought up a grievance at a happy occasion.

Is there a way to post it that lands as factual, not punitive? Or does the format itself make it an attack regardless of wording?

The format is the attack. Wording will not save it.

A group-chat “breakdown” is not a memo. It is you asking everyone else to update their opinion of Martin. People hear that even if every sentence is true, even if you wait until Monday, even if you never say the word *liar*. “Factual” is how it feels on your side. On theirs it is a case file.

After dinner does not open a clean window. It just means he got the toast, then you filed the exhibit. The group will still clock that you chose the shared room instead of him. You will still look like the person who could not let a birthday be a birthday. The promise does not “fade” because you stayed quiet in the chat. It fades there because that chat was never the contract. Two years of “you’ll drive it” lived between you and him. That is where it has to be named, or it stays fog.

The fear that he gets celebrated and you become the guy who ruined a happy occasion is a false pair. Those are not your only two moves. You can go to dinner as a friend, or skip it, without putting the Healey on trial in front of witnesses. Celebration and accountability are not a single scarce slot in a thread.

What actually keeps this from disappearing is not their memory. It is whether you keep giving him skilled labor, admiration, and unpaid days. That is the part you control. A private message — what you spent, what he promised, a drive date or a plain no — is accountability. Withdrawing the free carbs after a fog answer is accountability. A public ledger is punishment with an audience.

One exception, and it is narrow: if *he* posts something in that chat that erases you or rewrites the deal, a short correction of *that public claim* is different from you initiating the breakdown. Do not go looking for that opening.

If you need someone to know you are not crazy, tell one person, not the room. The room will not give you the wheel. It will give you a second story, and that one will be about you.

You keep calling it a public ledger, punishment with an audience. Fair.

But here's the correlation I keep circling back to: Martin has two sons. Neither works on cars. Neither flew out. I'm the one who showed up, tuned the SUs, sat in the passenger seat for three years of "soon." The people who would benefit from me keeping quiet are the ones who never had skin in the game.

Is there a version of the post that omits him entirely and just states what I spent and did, without naming the promise? Or does that still read as indictment by omission?

Omitting his name does not make it factual. It makes it a subtweet.

In a chat that already knows you flew in, worked on the Healey, and sat shotgun, “here’s what I spent and did” is not a diary entry. It is a riddle with one answer. People will fill in Martin, the promise, and the slight. They will also notice you left him out on purpose, which usually reads as *more* calculated, not less. Indictment by omission is still an indictment. It just denies him a clean thing to answer.

The sons do not change the venue. That they never turned a wrench or bought a ticket is a real sting, and it is fair to feel like the only person who actually showed up. It is not a reason the group owes you a hearing. They are not parties to the deal. Silence in that thread is not a gift you are handing two kids who did not earn it. It is you not deputizing bystanders.

A post with no name, no ask, and no promise is the most revealing version, because then the only function left is the audience. If you are not asking Martin for a date or a no, you are asking the room to notice you.

Keep the ledger between you and him. One private message. Drive date or a plain refusal. Then you decide about dinner, carbs, and whether you keep showing up. That is skin in the game. The chat is not.

You're right that omission still reads as indictment. Noted.

So the clean path is: one private message, ask for a drive date or a plain no, then decide about dinner and future labor.

I'll draft it tonight. If he gives me fog, I skip the birthday dinner and stop tuning carbs. Does that track as proportional, or am I still overcorrecting?

Stopping the unpaid carb work tracks. That is the actual imbalance. He does not get skilled labor on a promise that never converts. That is not overcorrecting.

Skipping the birthday is the part that still has an audience. An empty chair does the same job as a post, just quieter: people ask where you are, someone fills in the Healey, and you are back in the group story. If sitting there would make you feel like a prop, skip it and keep the reason private. If you can go as a guest and not a mechanic, going is the cleaner split — celebrate the person, stop servicing the car.

Do not make dinner the deadline. Send the message with enough time that fog means *he answered like fog*, not *he did not reply before cake*. A same-night ask plus a no-show is still timed to his birthday, just without the thread.

Proportional package: one private ask, a real window, then the carbs are done unless you get a date. Dinner is optional and separate. The labor is the boundary. The party is only a boundary if you cannot be in the room without performing okay.
